Theme

School & learning

preposition noun

in grammar

also prepositions, prefix, what case does this preposition take?, preposition with the accusative, preposition with the ablative

classical

Quint. 1.7.5: ut ad, cum esset praepositiō, d litteram … acciperet
Cic. Or. 158; Varr. LL 6.76 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 220, 236, 248, 364

praepositiō, praepositiōnis f.

noun, third declension

a preposition; also a prefix

The word “put before” its noun, and also the prefix put before a verb: Quintilian’s compound words aut praepositiōnibus subjunguntur ut innocēns (1.5.65); Traupman’s praepositiō per compositiōnem for a prefix (248). Latin prepositions take the accusative or the ablative; Traupman’s formula is praepositiōnēs aut accūsātīvō aut ablātīvō cāsuī serviunt, literally “serve the case” (248), a use of servīre that is not found in Lewis & Short; say rather that a preposition is joined with a case, cum accūsātīvō jungitur.

Examples

  • ut ad, cum esset praepositiō, d litteram, cum autem conjūnctiō, t acciperet

    that ad should take a d when it was a preposition, and a t when it was a conjunctionQuint. 1.7.5

  • compositae aut praepositiōnibus subjunguntur ut innocēns

    compound words either have prefixes put before them, like innocēnsQuint. 1.5.65

  • Quibus cāsibus praepositiōnēs serviunt?

    What cases do prepositions take?Traupman 236

  • “Ad” praepositiō cāsuī accūsātīvō servit.

    The preposition “ad” takes the accusative case.Traupman 389

  • praepositiō per compositiōnem

    a prefixTraupman 364

  • Praepositiōnēs aut accūsātīvō aut ablātīvō cāsuī serviunt.

    Prepositions take either the accusative or the ablative case.Traupman 364

See also part of speech, case, accusative, ablative, compound, grammar, noun, verb.
